sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (source: AAP Committee on Nutrition, last updated 4/26/2018)
sources.quote: Serve one meal for the whole family and resist the urge to make another meal if your child refuses what you've served. This only encourages picky eating. Try to include at least one food your child likes with each meal and continue to provide a balanced meal, whether she eats it or not. ... Just because a child refuses a food once, don't give up. Keep offering new foods and those your child didn't like before. It can take as many as 10 or more times tasting a food before a toddler’s taste buds accept it. Scheduled meals and limiting snacks can help ensure your child is hungry when a new food is introduced. ... To minimize waste, offer new foods in small amounts and wait at least a week or two before reintroducing the same food. ... Let you child pick which fruit and vegetable to make for dinner or during visits to the grocery store or farmer's market. ... Some cooking tasks are perfect for toddlers (with lots of supervision, of course): sifting, stirring, counting ingredients ... Help your child explore new flavors and textures in food.
sources.supports: Include at least one liked food at each meal; it can take 10 or more tastes before a toddler accepts a food; offer new foods in small amounts and wait a week or two before offering the same food again; let the child pick a vegetable at the store; toddlers can help with stirring and counting; help children explore new flavors and textures. Written for toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Toddlers at the Table: Avoiding Power Struggles
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: Especially with foods that aren't yet favorites, a couple of tablespoons is plenty to start with. Small portions are less overwhelming
sources.supports: Small portions of new foods (a couple of tablespoons) are less overwhelming. Written about toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Fussy eaters
sources.publisher: NHS (page last reviewed 13 November 2023)
sources.quote: The best way for your child to learn to eat and enjoy new foods is to copy you. Try to eat with them as often as you can. ... Changing how you serve a food may make it more appealing. For example, your child might refuse cooked carrots but enjoy raw grated carrot.
sources.supports: Children learn to eat new foods by copying their parents; changing how a food is served (raw grated carrot instead of cooked) may help. NHS advice for parents of fussy eaters (baby and toddler section); applied to ages 3 to 4.

sources.title: Peas, please! Food familiarization though picture books helps parents introduce vegetables into preschoolers' diets
sources.publisher: Owen L.H., Kennedy O.B., Hill C., Houston-Price C., Appetite 2018;128:32-43 (peer reviewed, University of Reading repository)
sources.quote: Repeated taste exposure is an established means of increasing children’s liking and intake of fruit and vegetables. However, parents find it difficult to offer children disliked foods repeatedly, often giving up after a few attempts. Studies show that familiarizing children to fruit and vegetables through picture books can increase their interest in tasting targeted foods. ... compared to the control group who experienced only taste exposure, looking at vegetable books enhanced children’s liking of their target vegetable post-intervention (p<.001) and at follow-up (p<.05), and increased consumption of the vegetable at follow-up (p<.01).
sources.supports: Picture books that make a vegetable familiar raised toddlers' interest in tasting it and their liking of it. A randomised study with 127 toddlers aged 21 to 24 months; picture books about one target vegetable, read daily for two weeks before taste exposure. It does not test personalised books.

sources.title: Toddlers at the Table: Avoiding Power Struggles
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: Toddlers are learning to navigate their world, communicate, and control some parts of their lives. They don't actually have control over much, but eating is one of the first areas where they will. ... They need to decide whether to eat, what they will eat, and how much to eat. ... Then present two healthy snack options to choose from. Even a child who is sad about the lack of candy will still enjoy the sense of control from deciding which healthy snack to eat. ... Or you might start bargaining: "If you eat 3 more bites, I'll give you a cookie." The problem is that these tactics don't work in the long run. ... Threatening a punishment, much like bribing a child with dessert, won't work in the long run either. It creates a power struggle.
sources.supports: Eating is one of the first areas where toddlers have control; they need to decide whether to eat, what and how much; offering two healthy options gives a sense of control; bargaining for bites and threatening punishment do not work in the long run and create a power struggle. The two-options line is about snacks; we apply it to vegetables at a meal. Written about toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (source: AAP Committee on Nutrition, last updated 4/26/2018)
sources.quote: It's a parent's responsibility to provide food, and the child’s decision to eat it. Pressuring kids to eat, or punishing them if they don't, can make them actively dislike foods they may otherwise like.
sources.supports: A parent's responsibility to provide food and the child's decision to eat it; pressuring kids to eat can make them dislike foods. Written for toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Fussy eaters
sources.publisher: NHS (page last reviewed 13 November 2023)
sources.quote: Do not use food as a reward. Your child may start to think of sweets as nice and vegetables as nasty. ... If your child rejects the food, do not force them to eat it. Just take the food away without saying anything. Try to stay calm, even if it's very frustrating. Try the food again another time.
sources.supports: Do not use food as a reward (sweets become nice and vegetables nasty); if a child rejects a food, take it away without saying anything and try again another time. NHS advice for parents of fussy eaters (baby and toddler section); applied to ages 3 to 4.

sources.title: How Should I Deal With a Picky Eater?
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: Telling kids they can have a cookie if they eat their broccoli only reinforces the appeal of the cookie over the veggies.
sources.supports: A cookie for eating broccoli only reinforces the appeal of the cookie over the vegetables. A parent Q&A about a picky eater who wants the same food every day.

sources.title: Peas, please! Food familiarization though picture books helps parents introduce vegetables into preschoolers' diets
sources.publisher: Owen L.H., Kennedy O.B., Hill C., Houston-Price C., Appetite 2018;128:32-43 (peer reviewed, University of Reading repository)
sources.quote: Repeated taste exposure is an established means of increasing children’s liking and intake of fruit and vegetables. However, parents find it difficult to offer children disliked foods repeatedly, often giving up after a few attempts. Studies show that familiarizing children to fruit and vegetables through picture books can increase their interest in tasting targeted foods. ... compared to the control group who experienced only taste exposure, looking at vegetable books enhanced children’s liking of their target vegetable post-intervention (p<.001) and at follow-up (p<.05), and increased consumption of the vegetable at follow-up (p<.01).
sources.supports: Picture books that make a vegetable familiar raised toddlers' interest in tasting it and their liking of it. A randomised study with 127 toddlers aged 21 to 24 months; picture books about one target vegetable, read daily for two weeks before taste exposure. It does not test personalised books.

sources.publisher: NHS (page last reviewed 13 November 2023)
sources.quote: Ask an adult that your child likes and looks up to to eat with you. Sometimes a child will eat for someone else, such as a grandparent, without any fuss. ... The best way for your child to learn to eat and enjoy new foods is to copy you. Try to eat with them as often as you can. ... Make mealtimes enjoyable and not just about eating. Sit down and chat about other things. ... If you know any other children of the same age who are good eaters, ask them round for tea. But do not talk too much about how good the other children are. ... Do not leave meals until your child is too hungry or tired to eat.

Try to include at least one food your child likes with each meal and continue to provide a balanced meal, whether she eats it or not. ... Kids this age also tend to enjoy any food involving a dip.

sources.title: Risk Factors and Consequences of Food Neophobia and Pickiness in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review
sources.publisher: del Campo C. et al., Foods 2024;14(1):69 (systematic review, PMC)
sources.quote: Currently, neophobia is a useful mechanism in early childhood linked to the development of a sense of taste; the attitude of distrust toward novelty protects the child from the danger of eating something potentially dangerous to health ... Sensory characteristics have been reported as the most influential determinants of eating behavior, and among these, textures are the main reason for food rejection or acceptance in children ... Food neophobia is a natural development stage that usually resolves spontaneously
sources.supports: Wariness of new food is a useful mechanism in early childhood and a natural stage that usually resolves; texture is the main reason children reject or accept foods. A systematic review on food neophobia and pickiness; the quoted lines are its background statements.

sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (source: AAP Committee on Nutrition, last updated 4/26/2018)
sources.quote: Serve one meal for the whole family and resist the urge to make another meal if your child refuses what you've served. This only encourages picky eating. Try to include at least one food your child likes with each meal and continue to provide a balanced meal, whether she eats it or not. ... Once a food is accepted, use what nutritionists call "food bridges" to introduce others with similar color, flavor and texture to help expand variety in what your child will eat. ... Just because a child refuses a food once, don't give up. Keep offering new foods and those your child didn't like before. It can take as many as 10 or more times tasting a food before a toddler’s taste buds accept it. Scheduled meals and limiting snacks can help ensure your child is hungry when a new food is introduced. ... To minimize waste, offer new foods in small amounts and wait at least a week or two before reintroducing the same food. ... Try serving unfamiliar foods, or flavors young children tend to dislike at first (sour and bitter), with familiar foods toddlers naturally prefer (sweet and salty). Pairing broccoli (bitter) with grated cheese (salty), for example, is a great combination for toddler taste buds. ... Tempting as it may be, try not to bribe your children with treats for eating other foods. This can make the "prize" food even more exciting, and the food you want them to try an unpleasant chore. It also can lead to nightly battles at the dinner table. ... It's a parent's responsibility to provide food, and the child’s decision to eat it. Pressuring kids to eat, or punishing them if they don't, can make them actively dislike foods they may otherwise like.
sources.supports: Include one liked food at each meal; food bridges to foods of similar color, flavor and texture; 10 or more tastes; wait a week or two before offering the same food again; pair bitter vegetables with familiar salty foods such as broccoli with grated cheese; no treats as bribes; the parent provides and the child decides whether to eat. Written for toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Toddlers at the Table: Avoiding Power Struggles
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: You choose the foods on your toddler's plate — and you don't have to serve macaroni and cheese daily. If you do, you miss a chance to introduce new foods and increase the number of foods your child is willing to eat. Most of these "food jags" won't last long if parents don't give in to them. ... Especially with foods that aren't yet favorites, a couple of tablespoons is plenty to start with. Small portions are less overwhelming
sources.supports: The parent chooses what goes on the plate and need not serve the same favorite daily; most food jags don't last long; small portions of new foods. Written about toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Peas, please! Food familiarization though picture books helps parents introduce vegetables into preschoolers' diets
sources.publisher: Owen L.H., Kennedy O.B., Hill C., Houston-Price C., Appetite 2018;128:32-43 (peer reviewed, University of Reading repository)
sources.quote: Repeated taste exposure is an established means of increasing children’s liking and intake of fruit and vegetables. However, parents find it difficult to offer children disliked foods repeatedly, often giving up after a few attempts. Studies show that familiarizing children to fruit and vegetables through picture books can increase their interest in tasting targeted foods. ... compared to the control group who experienced only taste exposure, looking at vegetable books enhanced children’s liking of their target vegetable post-intervention (p<.001) and at follow-up (p<.05), and increased consumption of the vegetable at follow-up (p<.01).

sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (source: AAP Committee on Nutrition, last updated 4/26/2018)
sources.quote: It's a parent's responsibility to provide food, and the child’s decision to eat it. Pressuring kids to eat, or punishing them if they don't, can make them actively dislike foods they may otherwise like. ... Share a meal together as a family as often as you can. This means no media distractions like TV or cell phones at mealtime. Use this time to model healthy eating. ... Serve one meal for the whole family and resist the urge to make another meal if your child refuses what you've served. This only encourages picky eating. Try to include at least one food your child likes with each meal and continue to provide a balanced meal, whether she eats it or not. ... Try serving unfamiliar foods, or flavors young children tend to dislike at first (sour and bitter), with familiar foods toddlers naturally prefer (sweet and salty). Pairing broccoli (bitter) with grated cheese (salty), for example, is a great combination for toddler taste buds. ... Just because a child refuses a food once, don't give up. Keep offering new foods and those your child didn't like before. It can take as many as 10 or more times tasting a food before a toddler’s taste buds accept it. Scheduled meals and limiting snacks can help ensure your child is hungry when a new food is introduced. ... To minimize waste, offer new foods in small amounts and wait at least a week or two before reintroducing the same food. ... Let you child pick which fruit and vegetable to make for dinner or during visits to the grocery store or farmer's market. ... Some cooking tasks are perfect for toddlers (with lots of supervision, of course): sifting, stirring, counting ingredients ... Tempting as it may be, try not to bribe your children with treats for eating other foods. This can make the "prize" food even more exciting, and the food you want them to try an unpleasant chore. It also can lead to nightly battles at the dinner table.
sources.supports: The parent provides food and the child decides whether to eat; pressure can make children dislike foods; family meals with no TV or phones; one meal for the whole family with one liked food; pair bitter vegetables with familiar salty foods; 10 or more tastes; scheduled meals and limiting snacks; wait a week or two before offering the same food again; let the child pick vegetables and help cook; no bribes, which turn the new food into a chore and lead to battles. Written for toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Toddlers at the Table: Avoiding Power Struggles
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: A parent's role is to present healthy foods and let a child decide which ones to eat — or whether to eat at all. ... Avoid offering snacks or giving hungry kids cups of milk or juice right before a meal. This can lessen their appetite and make them less willing to try a new food being offered. ... Threatening a punishment, much like bribing a child with dessert, won't work in the long run either. It creates a power struggle.
sources.supports: A parent presents foods and lets the child decide which to eat or whether to eat; a couple of tablespoons of new food is plenty; no snacks, milk or juice right before a meal; threats, like bribes, create a power struggle. Written about toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (source: AAP Committee on Nutrition, last updated 4/26/2018)
sources.quote: For weeks, they may eat 1 or 2 preferred foods – and nothing else. ... If you are concerned about your child’s diet, talk with your pediatrician, who can help troubleshoot and make sure your child is getting all the necessary nutrients to grow and develop. Also keep in mind that picky eating usually is a normal developmental stage for toddlers. ... Just because a child refuses a food once, don't give up. Keep offering new foods and those your child didn't like before. It can take as many as 10 or more times tasting a food before a toddler’s taste buds accept it. Scheduled meals and limiting snacks can help ensure your child is hungry when a new food is introduced. ... Serve one meal for the whole family and resist the urge to make another meal if your child refuses what you've served. This only encourages picky eating. Try to include at least one food your child likes with each meal and continue to provide a balanced meal, whether she eats it or not. ... Try serving unfamiliar foods, or flavors young children tend to dislike at first (sour and bitter), with familiar foods toddlers naturally prefer (sweet and salty). Pairing broccoli (bitter) with grated cheese (salty), for example, is a great combination for toddler taste buds. ... To minimize waste, offer new foods in small amounts and wait at least a week or two before reintroducing the same food. ... It's a parent's responsibility to provide food, and the child’s decision to eat it. Pressuring kids to eat, or punishing them if they don't, can make them actively dislike foods they may otherwise like.
sources.supports: For weeks toddlers may eat 1 or 2 preferred foods and nothing else; picky eating is usually a normal developmental stage; talk with your pediatrician if concerned; 10 or more tastes; one liked food at each meal; pair bitter vegetables with familiar salty foods; small amounts and a week or two before trying the same food again; pressure can make children dislike foods. Written for toddlers; applied to ages 3 to 4 as the same stage.

sources.title: Fussy eaters
sources.publisher: NHS (page last reviewed 13 November 2023)
sources.quote: But it's perfectly normal for toddlers to refuse to eat or even taste new foods. ... Do not worry about what your child eats in a day or if they do not eat everything at mealtimes. It's more helpful to think about what they eat over a week. ... If your child is active and gaining weight, and they seem well, then they're getting enough to eat. ... As long as your child eats some food from the 4 main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; dairy or dairy alternatives; and beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins) you do not need to worry. ... Children's tastes change. One day they'll hate something, but a month later they may love it.
sources.supports: Refusing new foods is normal for toddlers; think about what they eat over a week; an active child who is gaining weight and seems well is getting enough; some food from the 4 main food groups (including rice and pasta) means no need to worry; tastes change. NHS advice for parents of fussy eaters (baby and toddler section); applied to ages 3 to 4.

sources.title: Peas, please! Food familiarization though picture books helps parents introduce vegetables into preschoolers' diets
sources.publisher: Owen L.H., Kennedy O.B., Hill C., Houston-Price C., Appetite 2018;128:32-43 (peer reviewed, University of Reading repository)
sources.quote: Repeated taste exposure is an established means of increasing children’s liking and intake of fruit and vegetables. However, parents find it difficult to offer children disliked foods repeatedly, often giving up after a few attempts. Studies show that familiarizing children to fruit and vegetables through picture books can increase their interest in tasting targeted foods. ... compared to the control group who experienced only taste exposure, looking at vegetable books enhanced children’s liking of their target vegetable post-intervention (p<.001) and at follow-up (p<.05), and increased consumption of the vegetable at follow-up (p<.01).
sources.supports: Picture books that make a vegetable familiar raised toddlers' interest in tasting it and their liking of it. A randomised study with 127 toddlers aged 21 to 24 months; picture books about one target vegetable, read daily for two weeks before taste exposure. It does not test personalised books.
